title: Peter Chrysologus (30 July)
hook: golden-worded bishop of Ravenna known for short sermons
tomorrow: Our Lady of the Snows (5 August)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha, Mary and Lazarus, the household at Bethany. Your line was the house at bethany. Who will you welcome to your table? Day one thousand thirteen.

A sermon that ends while people are still paying attention. Not the homily that circles the runway before it lands. Today's saint aimed for the first kind. He was a bishop in the Italian city of Ravenna, he preached often, and tradition remembers him for keeping it short, so his people wouldn't tire and lose the thread. Somewhere along the way he was given a second name, a nickname that stuck so well it replaced his own. Today, the bishop with the golden word.
screen: `A SERMON THAT ENDS IN TIME.` → `A BISHOP OF RAVENNA.` → `A NICKNAME THAT STUCK.`

segments.voice: His name was Peter. Chrysologus came later. It's Greek, and tradition says it means golden-worded, a title given for the way he spoke. Sermons under his name have come down to us, and they are brief. One idea, opened up, and done. A line from the wisdom books fits him. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says: "therefore let thy words be few." The verse gives its reason just before: God is in heaven, and you are on earth. Few words aren't a lack of things to say. They're a kind of respect, for God and for the person listening. One of the sermons attributed to him is still read in the Church's prayer during Lent. It ties three practices together: prayer, fasting and mercy. In his picture they belong to each other and shouldn't be pulled apart. Prayer knocks, fasting obtains, mercy receives. If you pray but never show mercy, he says in effect, you've cut the thread. He fits a lot into a small space. That's the gift of a short word: it has to carry weight, so you choose it carefully. The Church honors him as a teacher of the faith, and a whole teaching is folded into his nickname. Say what is true, say it well, and stop. Gold is heavy. A little goes a long way.
screen: `PETER, THEN CHRYSOLOGUS.` · `ONE IDEA, AND DONE.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, MERCY TOGETHER.` · `SAY IT WELL, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `THEREFORE LET THY WORDS BE FEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one short, true sentence. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you need to say something to. Maybe it's thank you. Maybe it's sorry, or I'm proud of you, or I'm worried. Now cut it down. No speech, no explanation. Just the sentence, as few words as it can hold. Turn it over until it's simple and true. If you pray, you can offer God a short word too, as few words as you like. If you don't, simply rest in the quiet after the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Peter Chrysologus. A bishop of Ravenna whose short sermons earned him a Greek nickname that tradition says means golden-worded.
Your line: short and golden. Today, say your one short, true sentence to the person it's for, and then stop talking. Day one thousand thirteen.

screen: `DAY 1013 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OUR LADY OF THE SNOWS.`

howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of Saint Peter Chrysologus on 30 July, and a sermon attributed to him on prayer, fasting and mercy is read in the Liturgy of the Hours during Lent.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording and numbering of Ecclesiastes 5:1 (5:2 in some Bibles).
'Chrysologus means golden-worded' is attributed to 'the usual account'; confirm.
'His sermons have come down to us' and 'tradition remembers him for keeping it short': confirm.

Sermon 43 on prayer, fasting and mercy, read in the Office of Readings in Lent: paraphrased only (modern translations are not public domain). 'Prayer knocks, fasting asks, mercy receives' is a paraphrase; confirm it is faithful.
'The Church honors him as a teacher of the faith' stands in for Doctor of the Church; confirm whether to name the title.
